lawyer:
S.S. Halder with R.C. Maitra, Advocates ------  For the Appellant. 
Mvi. Md. Wahidullah with Firoj Shah and Aminul Islam Mondal, Advocates ------ For the Accused-Respondent Nos. 4 and 5.  
S.B. Barua, Advocate ------  For the State.
parties:
Monindra Kumar Malaker ------ Appellant 
Vs. 
The State ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque, J.:-This Criminal Appeal No. 215 of 1989 (previously Criminal Revision No. 94 of 1989) is directed against the judgment and order of acquittal dated 29.1.89 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal, Gazipur, in Special Tribunal Case No. 13 of 1986 acquitting the accused-respondent Nos. 4 and 5 from the charge under section 366A of the Penal Code read with section 4 (b) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 (Ordinance No. LX of 1983). 

 2. By an order dated 2.4.89 this case was directed to be heard along with Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 57 of 1987. So, both the cases are heard together by us, but for the sake of convenience we are giving two separate judgments in two cases. 

 3. Before discussing the prosecution case it may be mentioned that against the aforesaid judgment of acquittal the present appellant (being informant-father of victim girl) preferred an appeal before this court being Criminal Appeal No. 55 of 1989 within time under section 30 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. The matter as regards maintainability of the appeal was heard by a Division Bench (Fazle Hossain Mohammad Habibur Rahman and Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury, JJ) on 20th February, 1989. The above Division Bench relying on a decision reported in 40 DLR 161 held that the informant-appellant was not competent under the Special Powers Act to prefer an appeal under section 30 against judgment of acquittal passed by the Special Tribunal and on that ground the Division Bench dismissed the appeal summarily. Further, the above Division Bench observed that an application under section 561A Cr. P.C. could be preferred by the informant against the judgment of acquittal. In pursuance of the above order the present appellant preferred an application under section 561 A of Cr.P.C. before this Court and a Rule was issued on 2.4.89 by a Division Bench in which Justice Fazle Hossain Mohammad Habibur Rahman was a party and the said application under section 561A Cr.P.C. was registered as Criminal Revision No. 94 of 1989. 

 4. At the time of hearing of the Criminal Revision No. 94 of 1989 along with Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 57 of 1987 it appeared to us that in a case reported in 34 DLR (AD) 309 their Lordships of the Appellate Division expressed a view that against a judgment of acquittal the State or the aggrieved person may prefer an appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act. Relying upon the aforesaid decision this Bench passed an order on 9.8.89 treating the Criminal Revision No. 94 of 1989 as Criminal Appeal No. 215 of 1989 and held that the present petitioner Monindra Kumar Malaker being informant and father of the victim girl in the above criminal case is competent to prefer appeal against the judgment of acquittal under the Special Powers Act. Regarding maintainability of this appeal or the application under section 561A Cr. P.C. we will discuss in details later on. 

 5. The prosecution case is that the informant P.W. 1 Monindra Kumar Malakar is the father of the victim girl. He lodged First Information Report in Kaliakoir Police Station on 20.2.86 alleging, inter alia, that in the night following 15.2.86 at about 3/ 3-30 A.M. his daughter Uma Rani Malakar aged about 12/13 years went out of the room in order to answer the call of nature. As she was not returning to the but he and other people of the village searched for her at different places. Ultimately, from some people he came to know that accused Nawshed Bepari and Wahab Bepari and other people of bad character took away his minor daughter through fear and inducement and she was kept in their custody against her will. It is further apprehended that the accused would commit rape against the will of his minor daughter and do other harm to her. As he was busy to search his daughter he could not lodge the FIR earlier and on that date he sent the written FIR to the Police Station through his son Dhiman. The police started a case under section 366A of the Penal Code and section 4(b) of Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 hereinafter referred to as the said Ordinance No. LX of 1983. The police subsequently arrested the accused Nawshed and the victim girl Uma Rani Malakar. After investigation police submitted charge sheet under the aforesaid provisions of law. Ultimately the case was sent to the Special Tribunal for trial as an offence under section 4(b) of Ordinance No. LX of 1983 as triable under the Special Powers Act. 

 6. The prosecution examined as many as 10 witnesses, while the defence examined none. But its case, as it appears from the cross-examination, was that the accused did not take Uma Rani Malakar by force or inducement against her will. Uma Rani of her own accord embraced Islam and married Nawshed Bepari and as such they did not commit any offence as alleged against them. The Special Tribunal framed charges against the accused persons under the provisions of section 366A of the Penal Code read with section 4(b) of the said Ordinance. After perusing the materials on record and hearing the parties the Special Tribunal, by its judgment dated 29.1.89, acquitted the accused from the aforesaid charges. 

 7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgement of acquittal the present appellant Monindra Kumar Malakar, the informant of the case and father of the victim girl Uma Rani Malakar, preferred this appeal. 

 9. P.W. 1 is the informant himself. In his evidence he has reiterated what he stated in the First Information Report. He further stated that in the next morning the mother-in-law of accused Wahab stated to him secretly that Uma Rani was taken away by Nowshed. Thereafter, this informant along with his neighbour Amir Hossain went to the house of Nawshed and stated the above occurrence to Akbar, the eldest brother of Nawshed. At that time accused Wahab requested him not to start any case and he assured that he would bring them from Chowrasta. Thereafter he did not contact Nawshed and Uma Rani. A few days after, on one Tuesday, he came to know from accused Wahab that Nawshed and Uma Rani married each other in Court at Sirajganj Upazila. Next day i.e. on Wednesday he lodged F.I.R. in the police station. When he lodged the First Information Report in police Station the girl was 12 or 13 years old. One year after independence of Bangladesh she was born. He stated that Uma Rani Malakar was his 5th issue and her horoscope was given to the police. In cross-examination he stated that in his village Muslims are majority. He mixed with them. Uma Rani read in the free primary school where both boys and girls are reading together. His eldest daughter was married. She was taken to India and given in marriage there. After 1971 the aforesaid marriage took place. After the occurrence his 3rd, 4th and 5th daughters were sent to India. His daughter did not go to the house of the Muslims of his village. After 25 days from the date of occurrence Nawshed and Uma Rani were arrested at the village Dhirasram. After their arrest his daughter Uma Rani did not go to his house and she was produced before the Upazila Magistrate after 7 days from the date of arrest for 3 days after their arrest Uma Rani was always crying. He filed an application before the Upazila Magistrate for taking the custody of Uma Rani Malakar and made statement before the Magistrate. Although the Upazila Magistrate directed Uma Rani to go with him she was reluctant to go with him. His wife went to Gazipur Jail twice to see Uma Rani. He denied the suggestion that the horoscope was forged and fabricated and that one Ahsanullah died in his house after taking wine. He further denied the suggestion that he asked his daughters to supply wine to other persons in his house and for that reason his daughter went away from his house and embraced Islam and married Nawshed. He also denied that for his above activities his daughter was dissatisfied. 

 16 P.W. 9 Abu Reza was the I.O. in the case. He stated that on 20.2.86 he was in Kaliakoir Police Station. He investigated the present case and submitted charge-sheet against the accused persons under section 366A of the Penal Code and section 4(b) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983. Before submitting charge sheet he went to the place of occurrence, prepared sketch map and index of the place of occurrence and took statement of the witnesses under section 161 Cr.P.C. and then submitted charge sheet. He recovered the victim girl Uma Rani from a vacant house at village Kishoregram within Joydebpur police station and Nawshed was arrested from there. Thereafter Uma Rani was sent to judicial custody and Nawshed was sent to the Court. In cross-examination he stated that he went to the house of the informant after recording the F.I.R. The informant did not disclose to him about the date of birth of Uma Rani and that she was minor. Kartik Chandra Paul did not tell him that he saw Uma Rani in that night. Witnesses Shailabala Paul and Laxmi Rani did not state to him that at the time of birth of Uma Rani they were present. At the time of recovery of Uma Rani her father was with him. The statement of Uma Rani was recorded by the Magistrate. After recovery Uma Rani refused to go with her father and she claimed herself as major. He denied the suggestion that he submitted a false charge-sheet against the accused persons. 

 19. We will discuss the evidence on merit later on. At the outset let us consider the preliminary objection raised by the learned Advocate Mr. Wahidullah appearing for the respondent Nos. 4 and 5. The learned Advocate submits that an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure against an order of acquittal passed by the Special Tribunal does not lie before this Court, because at the relevant time no proceeding was pending which required quashment by this Court nor there was any chance of abuse of the process of the Court as the proceeding terminated with the pronouncement of the judgment. We find substance in the contention of Mr. Wahidullah. In our order dated 9.8.89 we have already held that in a case like this an application for quashing the proceeding under section 561A Cr.P.C. did not lie, rather we hold that an appeal against an order of acquittal passed by a Special Tribunal can be preferred either by the state or by any person aggrieved by that order. We passed the above order following a decision of their Lordships of the Application Division reported in 34 DLR(AD) 309 and thereafter we converted the application under section 561A Cr.P.C. to a Memorandum of Appeal. We have heard this mother as an appeal against the judgment of acquittal. 

 20. Mr. Wahidullah further submits that this appeal at the instance of the informant under section 30 of the Special Powers Act does not lie. The present appellant Monindra Kumar Malakar is simply an informant and he may be a witness in the case. On his F.I.R. the police investigated into the case, submitted charge-sheet and on the report of police Special Tribunal took cognizance and heard the case and disposed it of. So State is the complainant, like other criminal cases, in the present case and as such the appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act by the informant is incompetent. 

 21. In support of his contention Mr. Wahidullah has referred to the case of Firoza Begum Vs. Hormuz Ali & another, 40 DLR 161. In that case this point that an appeal under section 30(I) of the Special Powers Act at the instance of the informant did not lie when the accused are acquitted by the Special Tribunal was specifically mooted and argued. The aforesaid Division Bench (Fazle Hussain Mohammad Habibur Rahman and Abdul Bari Sarkar, JJ) held that the state and the accused are the only two competent parties in a case under the Special Powers Act, 1974. The State or the accused alone can file appeal under section 30(I) of the Special Powers Act against the judgment of the Special Tribunal. It is further held that the appeal at the instance of the informant is not maintainable under section 30 of the Special Powers Act. It is difficult for us to accept the above contention of Mr. Wahidullah, although he is relying upon a Division Bench decision of this Court, because of the fact that before the aforesaid Division Bench, we believe, the above decision of the Appellant Division was not placed. 

 22. A few days back while we were hearing a similar Criminal Case, one learned Advocate of this Bar Mr. Amjad Hossain had drawn our attention to the aforesaid decision of the Appellate Division inasmuch as in his case the similar question arose as to whether by an informant an appeal against a judgment of acquittal could be preferred before this Court under section 30 of the Special Powers Act. In the case of Abdul Halim Mollah alias Monohar Mollah and another Vs. The Member, Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka and others, 34 DLR(AD) 309 the specific question arose whether an appeal would lie against an order of acquittal passed by the Special Tribunal under the Special Powers Act. By a majority judgment (3:1) (while Mr. Justice Badrul Haider Chowdhury was dissenting) it was held that an appeal would lie against any judgment of the Special Tribunal whether it is a judgment of acquittal or a judgment of conviction. In deciding the aforesaid case a question arose before their Lordships as to who could prefer an appeal against a judgment of acquittal. In considering that point their Lordships held as follows:— 

 "Competency of appeal against orders of acquittal has not been challenged ever since. Similarly the scope of appeal as provided in sub-section (I) of section 30 of Special Powers Act is wide enough to include an appeal from orders of acquittal. If the view canvassed by the learned Counsel is accepted, it will lead to an inevitable complication, that is, in a case where the judgment which terminates the case in acquittal, and the evidence on record does not warrant the judgment or it is a perverse judgment, the State or the person aggrieved will have no remedy against such an illegal order of acquittal and consequently the accused will go unpunished, occasioning failure of justice. So, considering the question by applying any of the tests indicated above, I have no doubt that the word' judgment' occurring in sub-section (I) of section 30 of the Special Powers Act includes both judgment of conviction and judgment of acquittal. Appeals from judgments of acquittal: lie to the Appellate Tribunal; and if the Appellate Tribunal is satisfied on consideration of evidence that the order of acquittal cannot be sustained, it is competent to record its judgment of conviction on setting aside the judgment of acquittal. In that view of the matter the action of the Appellate Tribunal in entertaining appeal from order of acquittal and recording an order of conviction on setting aside the judgment of acquittal passed by the Special Tribunal, Patuakhali is in accordance with law, and the Appellate Tribunal was competent to pass the order of conviction on setting aside the judgment and order of the Special Tribunal acquitting the respondents and the High Court Division committed no error of law in dismissing the writ petition." 

 23. In the above case the accused were acquitted by the Special Tribunal. Then the State preferred an appeal against the above judgment of acquittal before the Appellate. Tribunal, which after hearing the parties allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of the Special Tribunal and convicted and sentenced the accused under section 395 of the Penal Code. On a Writ Petition High Court Division also upheld the above conviction and sentence. Lastly, the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court also dismissed the appeal maintaining the judgment passed by the High Court Division. 

 24. From the aforesaid decision it becomes quite clear to us that their Lordships are of the view that against a judgment of acquittal passed by the Special Tribunal either the State or any person aggrieved by such order of acquittal can prefer an appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act. In the present case the informant appellant is the father of the victim girl. He lodged the FIR and he is P.W. 1 in the case. The accused were acquitted by the Special Tribunal. In view of the above decision of the Appellate Division we have no hesitation to hold that the present appellant (informant P.W. 1. Monindra Kumar Malakar, the father of the victim girl) is definitely an aggrieved person and he is competent to prefer the present appeal against the judgment of acquittal passed by the Special Tribunal. So the objection raised by Mr. Wahidullah is over rulled. 

 25. Since we are differing from the views of another Division Bench of this Court on the self-same point of law, as a matter of rule, we require to send the matter to the learned Chief Justice recommending to constitute a Full Bench in order to decide the matter finally. But in the present case it is not necessary because we, relying upon the above decision of the Appellate Division, are holding that either the State or any person aggrieved can prefer an appeal under section 30 against a judgment of acquittal passed by the Special Tribunal. We believe the above decision of the Appellate Division was not placed before the Division Bench when it heard and decided the above case as reported in 40 DLR 161. 

 26. Let us now analyse the evidence adduced by the prosecution in this case. 

 P.W.I is the father and P.W. 2 is the brother of the victim girl. From their evidence it appears that at the time of occurrence the victim girl was aged about 12 or 13 years. In order to substantiate their statements the prosecution examined P.W. 3 Majibur Rahman, the Head Master of Kaliakoir Government Primary School who stated that on 14.2.86 he was the Head Master of the said Primary School and at that time the victim girl Uma Rani Malakar daughter of Monindra Kumar, Malakar was the student of Class V. In cross-examination he stated that Uma Rani Malakar read in that school without getting any admission and her name did not appear in admission register and there was no entry of her age and date of birth in the admission register. It is difficult to accept such an evidence which has not disclosed any-thing regarding the date of birth or the age of the victim girl. The school certificate is generally accepted as an important piece of evidence but here in the present case the prosecution has totally failed to ascertain the date of birth or the age of the victim girl by producing any evidence. It is quite unbelievable that in a Government Primary School a girl could read there without getting herself admitted. Such type of evidence is not at all acceptable to the Court. So the statements of P.Ws. 1 and 2, who are the father and brother of the victim girl, regarding her age is not at all supported by the evidence of the Head Master P.W.3. 

 33. In Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 57 of 1987 under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure this Bench has already delivered a judgment holding that at the relevant time i.e. on 15.2.86 the victim girl was not less than 16 years old and as such she was treated as major and allowed to go anywhere with anybody she liked. So, in the present case, on the basis of the evidence on record, we also hold that the victim girl was not less than 16 years of age when she left the house of her father on 15.2.86, went with Nawshed and married Nawshed embracing Islam. 

 34. Mr. S.S. Haider the learned Advocate for the appellant, submits that in fife present case since charge was framed under section 366A of the Penal Code read with section 4(b) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983 the minority of a girl shall be fixed at below 18 years, which means if she is found below 18 years she shall be treated as minor for the purpose of this case. In order to consider the above submission of Mr. Halder let us quote sections 361 and 366A of the Penal Code and section 4(b) of the Cruelty to Women (Deterrent Punishment) Ordinance, 1983. 

 35. The main ingredients of section 366A are, -(a) the girl must be below 18 years, (b) there must be definite inducement from the accused, (c) there must be intention to force or seduce such a girl to illicit intercourse with another person and (d) it will be done against her will. Ingredient of section 4(b) of the Ordinance is that the woman is kidnapped with intent to compel her to marry any person against her will. All such ingredients of section 366A of the Penal Code and section 4(b) of the said Ordinance, we find, are totally absent in the present case and as such the proceeding was without jurisdiction. Mr. Halder was in wrong impression that since the Tribunal found the age of the girl in between 16 and 17 years at the relevant time the Tribunal accepted the position that the girl was minor as she was below 18 years and as such the provisions of section 366A of the Penal Code are applicable. 

 Mr. Wahidullah, on the other hand, submits that if the age of the girl is 16 years or above and if with her consent she is taken by the accused person, it will not be an offence under section 366A of the Penal Code or section 4(b) of the said Ordinance inasmuch as always the girl being major had the consent to go with the accused. If the girl is below 16 the father can claim the custody but if the girl is above 16 then she will be treated as major and she can go according to her free will. For the purpose of section 366A of the Penal Code the girl must be in between the age of 16 and 18 years. If she is above 16 but below 18 and if she is induced to go with the accused, and if no force is used it will not be an office under section 366A of the Penal Code and section 4(b) of the said Ordinance. In support of his contention Mr. Wahidullah has referred to the case of Abbas Bahara and another Vs. Emperor, AIR 1933 (Cal) 362 (Rankin, C.J. and Costello, J). In that decision their Lordships were of the view that if a person induces a girl of an age between 16 and 18 years without force or fraud to go from any place with intent to have illicit intercourse with himself he will not be guilty of any offence. The relevant portion of the aforesaid decision is quoted as under:— 

 "Now, the learned Judge told the jury that he did not agree that under section. 366A it was necessary to show that the illicit intercourse was to be with some other person besides the accused. It appears that, as the law now stands, the person who induces a girl of an age between the years 16 and 18 without force or fraud to go from any place with the intention that she will have illicit intercourse with himself does not commit any offence. The new section, however, makes it an offence in the case of such girl if she is induced by a person to go from any place with intent that she may be or knowing that it is likely that she will be, forced or seduced to illicit intercourse with another person. We have to see what the case is as regards each of the two appellants before us. The prosecution case as against the appellant Abbas apparently is that he was ultimately minded to get married to this girl if he could. She was a Hindu girl and he was a Mohammedan. The prosecution case however was that when this girl came away from her father's house with the accused she was taken from place to place and from house to house for a certain number of nights, and the learned Judge left it to the jury as it was a question for the jury to determine whether there was any intention of illicit intercourse. On the other hand, it is clear enough according to the prosecution case that the accused Abbas was taking the girl because he wanted apparently to marry her or to have illicit intercourse with her himself and therefore he is not guilty under S.366A and apparently not guilty also of any other offence the girl being over 16 and under 18 years of age." 

 36. Mr. Wahidullah has also referred to the case of Nurul Islam @ Nur Islam Vs. The State, 23 DLR(Dac)126. It is a single Bench decision wherein his Lordship has observed that if it is found that the woman alleged to have been kidnapped or abducted is a consenting party and no act was committed by the accused against her will, then the accused cannot be brought within the mischief of section 366 of the Penal Code. 

 37. Relying on the aforecited decisions Mr. Wahidullah submits that even if Uma Rani was below 18 at the relevant time, yet the prosecution has totally failed to prove that accused Nawshed induced Uma Rani and took her away with intention to force or seduce her to illicit intercourse with another person and as such section 366A of the Penal Code has no manner of application in the present case. We find substance in the above contention of Mr. Wahidullah. 

 38. In view of our discussions above we have no hesitation to hold that the ingredients of section 366A of the Penal Code and those of section 4(b) of the aforesaid Ordinance are totally absent in the present case and as such we do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment of acquittal passed by the Special Tribunal. 

 39. In the midst of delivering judgment Mr. S.S. Haider has referred to the case of Talukder Abdul Aziz Vs. The State, 35 DLR 127 and submitted that since the charge of non-schedule offence under section 366A of the Penal Code and the charge of schedule offence under section 4(b) of the Ordinance No. LX of 1983 were brought at a time and tried together by the Special Tribunal under the Special Powers Act, the judgment of the Special Tribunal cannot be sustained in law. Suddenly Mr. Halder has referenced to this decision without considering the consequence of it. Mr. Halder has forgotten that he has been supporting the prosecution case and as soon as he submits that the proceeding of non-schedule and schedule offences together does not lie, it cuts the very root of the prosecution case. Such a suicidal and reckless citation is not of any assistance to Mr. Halder rather it speaks that the present proceeding against the accused persons is without jurisdiction. However, we refrain ourselves from expressing any definite opinion on the above point in this case. 

 40. In any view of the matter, since we have held that the ingredients of section 366A of the Penal Code and those of section 4(b) of Ordinance No. LX of 1983 are not at all attracted in the facts and circumstances of the present case, the impugned judgment of acquittal passed by the Special Tribunal does not require any interference by us.
